opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest starting point is that I don't treat it as a yes-or-no question. Simulation isn't automatically "the foundation," and real-world data isn't automatically the gold standard either. The question I keep asking is: what does the robot brain actually need to learn, and which data source teaches that most efficiently?

I usually break it down along a few dimensions.

**First, scale and diversity.** A general-purpose brain needs exposure to an enormous range of situations: different objects, layouts, lighting, failure modes. Collecting that in the real world through teleoperation is slow and expensive, and you hit a ceiling fast. Simulation lets you generate variation essentially for free. If the bottleneck is coverage, simulation has a very strong case.

**Second, what kind of knowledge transfers.** Some things transfer from sim to real quite well, like spatial reasoning, task structure, sequencing, and understanding where things are and what needs to happen next. Other things transfer poorly, like contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, friction, and the subtle physics of grasping something soft or slippery. So I ask whether the capability we care about lives mostly in the high-level reasoning layer or in the low-level physical interaction layer. For the former, simulation is a great foundation. For the latter, you need real data, or at least real data to calibrate against.

**Third, how fast the sim-to-real gap is closing.** This is the part people sometimes underestimate. Rendering has become much more realistic, and generative models can now produce visual diversity that hand-built simulators never could. If the visual gap shrinks and the physics gets good enough for the tasks you care about, the economics shift dramatically toward simulation. So part of the decision is a bet on trajectory, not just on where things stand today.

**Fourth, the feedback loop.** Simulation gives you something real-world data rarely does: you can reset, replay, and evaluate at scale. For training a policy with reinforcement learning, or even just evaluating a model fairly across thousands of scenarios, that's enormously valuable. A brain you can't evaluate systematically is hard to improve.

In practice, my view is that the answer is a layered recipe. Use simulation, plus increasingly generated data, to build broad priors and the bulk of the experience. Use real-world data, which is smaller but high quality, to anchor the model in true physics and correct the systematic biases simulation introduces. Then keep a tight loop where real-world failures tell you what your simulator is getting wrong.

So the way I'd frame the decision is this. Simulation is the right foundation when it's the cheapest way to get the coverage you need *and* you have a credible plan for closing the gap on the parts it gets wrong. If you can't articulate that second part, you're building on sand, no matter how much data you generate.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation is a good foundation when it provides needed coverage and its remaining gaps can be closed for the tasks in question.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute a preference for starting with real robots to Yujun Shen or say that simulation’s limited task coverage is the reason.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and I think the honest answer is that I don't really treat it as a binary decision. It's more about understanding what simulation can and cannot give you, and then being very deliberate about where it sits in the pipeline.

Let me start with why we even look at simulation. If you think about how large language models got where they are, it's because the internet gave us a nearly free, nearly infinite corpus of human behavior in text form. Robotics has no equivalent. Real robot data is expensive, slow, and dangerous to collect at scale. You can't crawl the physical world. So simulation is attractive precisely because it promises that kind of scale: you can generate millions of trajectories overnight, randomize everything, reset for free, and nobody gets hurt.

But the question I keep asking the team is: scale of what, exactly? Scale is only valuable if the distribution you're scaling is actually close to the one you'll face at deployment. And that's where simulation gets tricky, because the gap shows up in places you don't expect. Everyone talks about visual realism, textures, lighting. Those matter, but in my experience they're the easier part now, especially with generative models closing the rendering gap. The harder gap is physics and contact. Deformable objects, friction, liquids, things slipping in a gripper. Those are where simulators are still fundamentally approximating, and a policy trained to exploit simulator quirks will fail in ways that look almost random in the real world.

So the way I actually decide is roughly three questions. First, what is the skill I want to learn, and how contact-rich is it? For navigation, for locomotion, for a lot of coarse manipulation, simulation has essentially already won. Legged robots are the clearest example. For fine manipulation with soft or small objects, I'm much more skeptical that sim alone gets you there. Second, do I have a way to measure the gap? If I can't run a real-world evaluation that tells me how much my sim performance transfers, then I'm flying blind, and more simulation data just gives me more confidence in something I can't verify. Third, what is simulation's role: is it the foundation, or is it the amplifier? Those are different.

And I'll say where I've landed personally. I don't think simulation should be the foundation of a general-purpose robot brain. I think the foundation has to be grounded in real data, including real robot data and also human video, because that's where the true distribution lives. But simulation is an extraordinary amplifier on top of that. Use real data to anchor what the world actually looks like and feels like, then use simulation to explore the long tail, to practice failure recovery, to cover the rare cases you'd never want to collect for real. Think of it less as a replacement for reality and more as a way to spend reality more efficiently.

There's one more thing I'd add, which is that the line between simulation and real data is blurring. When you have a world model that's learned from real video and can roll forward plausible futures, is that simulation? It's generated, but it's grounded in real statistics rather than hand-coded physics. I think that's where a lot of this goes. So the question five years from now might not be "sim or real" at all. It might be "how good is your learned model of the world, and how much do you trust it to teach you things you haven't directly experienced."

r001.rationale: The response says simulation is effective for tasks such as navigation, locomotion, and coarse manipulation, while judging its suitability by the skill and contact demands.

r002.rationale: The response favors real data, including robot data, as a foundation, but grounds that preference in real-world data matching the deployment distribution and simulation’s physics and contact gaps—not in simulation’s limited coverage of the tasks a general-purpose brain must support.

astra-6.text:
I would start with the capabilities we want the robot to learn, rather than assuming simulation is the right foundation for everything. A general-purpose robot needs to perceive, act, and recover when something unexpected happens. Simulation may support those capabilities very differently.

The key test is whether learning in simulation improves performance in the real world. Can the robot handle a new object, a different environment, or a task variation without extensive retraining? And when it fails, is that because it needs more experience, or because the simulator leaves out something essential, like the way a material deforms or contact behaves?

I would compare simulation-trained systems with systems trained on real data, and with mixtures of the two, under the same real-world tests. You also have to count the effort of building and validating the simulation. Generating more data is useful only if that data teaches the right things.

So I would treat simulation as a candidate foundation whose value has to be demonstrated through transfer. It gives you a way to practice broadly, but real-world experience has to keep checking whether that practice is useful.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation’s value must be demonstrated through transfer to real-world performance, with success across relevant tasks and variations; this communicates suitability when simulation handles the chosen scenario well.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute a preference to Yujun Shen for starting with real robots or explain that preference as a consequence of simulation’s limited task coverage.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start with the capabilities we want the robot to learn, and then ask which of those simulation can actually teach. For a general-purpose robot, that includes perception, physical interaction, and making decisions over long sequences of actions. A simulator can be useful for one of those and still be weak on another.

The key test is transfer. If we train on simulated data, does the robot become more capable in the real world—on objects, environments, and tasks it hasn’t seen before? I’d want to compare that against real-world training and a mixture of the two, using the same evaluation tasks and accounting for the cost of generating the data.

I’d also look carefully at what the robot gets wrong. If it learns a strategy that exploits an unrealistic contact model, adding more simulated examples may just reinforce the wrong behavior. But if simulation lets us vary environments, practice recovery, and explore situations that are difficult to collect safely, it can be very valuable.

So I wouldn’t make it a binary choice between simulation and real data. I’d use real-world performance to decide where simulation is helping, where it needs calibration, and where we still need direct experience.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation is useful when it can teach the chosen capabilities and is strong for the relevant scenario, with real-world transfer used to assess that.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute a preference for starting with real robots to Yujun Shen or say that simulation currently lacks coverage of the tasks a general-purpose robot brain should support.
